what_its_for: Lidocaine cream is a numbing medicine that helps relieve pain, itching, and discomfort on your skin. It is used for minor skin irritations, sunburns, insect bites, minor cuts, scrapes, hemorrhoids, and to numb the skin before a needle stick or minor skin procedure.
how_to_take: This medicine is applied directly to your skin. Wash and dry the affected area first. Apply a thin layer of cream to the area that hurts or itches and gently rub it in, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. For some procedures, a thicker layer may be applied and covered with a special dressing or plastic wrap — follow your doctor or nurse's instructions exactly. Wash your hands before and after applying the cream. Do not get it in your eyes, mouth, nose, or ears. Do not swallow it. Only use it on your skin or the area your doctor told you to use it on.
dosing: Use only as much cream as directed by your doctor or as stated on the package. For over-the-counter use, adults typically apply a small amount to the affected area up to 3 to 4 times a day as needed. Do not use more than directed, and do not apply it over large areas of your body unless your doctor tells you to. For children, always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as the dose depends on the child's age, weight, and the size of the area being treated.
missed_dose: Lidocaine cream is usually used only when needed for pain or discomfort, so there is not a set schedule in most cases. If your doctor gave you a specific schedule and you forget to apply it, use it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next application, skip the missed dose and continue as normal. Do not apply a double amount to make up for a missed application.
storage: Store lidocaine cream at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the cap tightly closed when not in use. Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not freeze it. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Check the expiration date on the tube and do not use it past that date.
what_to_avoid: Do not apply lidocaine cream to broken, infected, severely burned, or deeply wounded skin unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid getting the cream in your eyes, ears, mouth, or nose — if this happens, rinse right away with plenty of water. Do not cover the treated area with a tight bandage or plastic wrap unless your doctor specifically tells you to, as this can cause too much medicine to be absorbed into your body. Do not use it on large areas of skin without medical guidance. Avoid using more than the recommended amount, as too much lidocaine can be absorbed and cause serious side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: dizziness, feeling faint, or lightheadedness; confusion or difficulty thinking clearly; blurred vision; ringing in your ears; numbness or tingling spreading beyond the treated area; irregular or fast heartbeat; seizures; difficulty breathing; or severe skin redness, rash, or swelling where the cream was applied. Also call your doctor if your pain or skin condition does not improve after a few days of using the cream.
when_it_works: Lidocaine cream usually starts to numb the skin within 20 to 30 minutes after applying it. If it is being used before a needle stick or skin procedure, your doctor or nurse may ask you to apply it 30 to 60 minutes ahead of time for best results. For pain and itching relief, you should feel some comfort fairly quickly. If you do not notice any improvement, talk to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults and young children may absorb more lidocaine through the skin and may be more sensitive to side effects. Use with extra caution in these groups and always follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should ask their doctor before using lidocaine cream. People with liver problems or certain heart conditions should also talk to their doctor before use, as lidocaine may build up in the body more easily.
